title: Expressions with come and go
subtitle: come across, come to an end, go through, on the go
summary: Use the phrasal verbs and collocations built on come and go, including come to / come into and the many meanings of go on.

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs with come
rows: think of or suggest a solution

lesson.heading: come in sentences
lesson.text: Note that **come by** often suggests you want to know how something was obtained, and **come up with** is always followed by an idea, a plan or a solution.

examples.text: Did the meeting you were planning ever **come off**?
When do the exam results **come out**?
I must tell you about an important point which **came up** at the meeting.
Nothing can **come between** him and football.
I **came across** a lovely old vase in that junk shop.
How did you **come by** that bruise?
Sofia **came up with** a really good idea to raise money for charity.

lesson.heading: come to and come into

left.label: come to = arrive at
left.text: Use **come to** for reaching a point, especially the end of a process.
examples: The two sides have at last **come to an agreement**.
I found it hard, but in the end I **came to a decision**.
I have **come to the conclusion** that he was lying.
Traffic **came to a standstill** because of the snow.
The war finally **came to an end** in 2005.
It was difficult to **come to terms with** my failure.

right.label: come into = start or acquire
right.text: Use **come into** for beginning to exist, work or be seen.
examples: He **came into a fortune** when his uncle died.
The telephone first **came into existence** 150 years ago.
They say long skirts are **coming into fashion** again.
The new motorway will **come into operation** next March.
After two hours at sea, the island **came into sight**.
I rarely **come into contact with** native speakers.

lesson.note: Come to terms with something = acknowledge it and accept it psychologically.

lesson.heading: go on, go through, go for, go with
rows: happen; continue; pass (of time); go in advance; criticise or complain (go on at someone)
experience or endure; check carefully; be completed or approved

lesson.heading: go in sentences
lesson.text: **Go on** is the hardest of these because it has five meanings. Look at what follows it: *go on at someone* is always a criticism, *go on -ing* is always 'continue'.

examples.text: They **went on** working despite the noise.
He's always **going on at** me about my untidy hair.
Let's **go through** the plans once more.
The business deal did not **go through** in the end.
He really **went for** her when she dared to criticise him.
Those shoes don't **go with** that dress.

lesson.heading: Other expressions with go
rows: it is clear without being said
not have enough money to pay your debts

lesson.text: Come across a word = find it by chance. Get your point across = communicate it. Same particle, very different verbs.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the meaning of the verb in it.

pairs.left: He went on composing music till his eighties.
She used to go through his pockets every night.
The dog went for the postman.
We had planned a meeting but it never came off.
I came across a photo of my grandmother.
I wish you'd stop going on at me!

exercises.prompt: I was sure he'd go for a holiday in Greece rather than stay at home. Here go for means ...
Nobody has come up with a solution to the problem so far. Here come up with means ...
exercises.explanation: Come up with = think of or suggest a plan or solution.

exercises.prompt: When his grandmother dies, he'll come ___ a fortune.
exercises.explanation: Come into a fortune = receive money when someone dies.

exercises.prompt: After four years of fighting, the civil war finally came to an ___.
Halfway up the steep hill, the bus came to a ___.
exercises.explanation: Come to a standstill = stop completely.

exercises.prompt: They say that long skirts are coming into ___ again.
exercises.explanation: Come into fashion = start to be fashionable.

exercises.prompt: I found it very difficult to come to ___ with my failure.
exercises.explanation: Come to terms with something = accept it psychologically.

exercises.prompt: Does each phrase follow come to or come into?
I don't need to say that we wish you all the best. - It goes ___ that we wish you all the best.
exercises.explanation: It goes without saying = it is clear without being said.

exercises.prompt: They took a lot of trouble to avoid meeting each other. - They went to great ___ to avoid meeting each other.
exercises.explanation: Go to great lengths = take a lot of trouble.

exercises.statement: I've been on the go all day and I'm longing for a shower now.
exercises.explanation: Correct. On the go = very busy, on the move.

exercises.statement: I do hope he will go without saying of his new business.
exercises.explanation: I do hope he will make a go of his new business. Make a go of something = make a success of it.

exercises.prompt: Match each question with the natural response.

pairs.left: Why don't you and Ollie go on?
How did he come by so much money?
pairs.right: A rich aunt of his died.

pairs.left: What's the worst pain you've ever gone through?
Why did that factory close down?
When should I come round to your place?
